cases.title: Topolobampo Ammonia Plant: Threats Against Yoreme Opponents
cases.place: Topolobampo and Ohuira Bay, Sinaloa, Mexico
cases.point: Topolobampo port (approximate; plant site not separately confirmed)

lenders.name: KfW IPEX-Bank (Germany)
lenders.role: Member of the consortium financing the plant, by its own account. Rebelión, in an opinion article, says the loan was 863 million euros, closed in 2020 with a German state guarantee. The Coalition for Human Rights in Development says KfW IPEX-Bank invested USD 1.5 billion. KfW gives no figure and no bank document was found.

cases.conditions: Loan for a plant designed to make 2,200 tonnes of anhydrous ammonia a day and store 75,000 tonnes on site, about 88% built in May 2026 (Mexico News Daily). KfW says the client has committed to the Equator Principles.
cases.community: Eleven UN special rapporteurs wrote from 19 September 2025 to Mexico, GPO, KfW IPEX-Bank, Germany and Switzerland about attacks on and persecution of Mayo-Yoreme communities, citing an attempted kidnapping and disappearance of one defender and effects on sacred sites (Grupo Animal). The letter's own text was not found. Defenders Melina Maldonado Sandoval and Claudia Quintero Sandoval have reported intimidation and threats since 2024 (Rebelión). Quintero told Witness Radio of death threats, physical violence and criminalization, and of destruction of a fishing site 4,000 families depend on; she also passed on a reported loss of over 60% of local species, which the article does not verify. Damage to the bay is mostly a forecast: production is not due until 2027, and CIIDIR-Sinaloa research cited by opponents estimates shrimp output could fall by up to 60%, more than 500 tonnes a year (Mexico News Daily).
cases.outcome: Mexico's Supreme Court revoked the original permits in 2022 for lack of Indigenous consultation. Semarnat says most of the 15 communities consulted then backed the plant; those around Ohuira Bay (Ohuira, Paredones, Lázaro Cárdenas) rejected it (Expansión). A challenge to the current authorisation is pending before a federal administrative court (Business and Human Rights Centre). Protesters set up a round-the-clock camp at the port in 2026 and moved it to block the plant's access road on 15 June (Mexico News Daily). KfW says it has hired an independent consultancy to reassess the consultation.

cases.title: Mannar Wind Farm: Bird Deaths, and Fishers' and Flood Claims After ADB Loan
cases.place: Mannar Island, Northern Province, Sri Lanka
cases.point: Mannar Island (approximate; turbine rows not separately located)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: US$200 million sovereign-guaranteed loan approved 24 October 2017 for the wind farm on Mannar Island.

cases.conditions: Loan to the Ceylon Electricity Board for the first phase, the 103.5 MW Thambapavani wind farm, which opened in 2020.
cases.community: The government's environmental impact report recorded 376 bird carcasses near the plant from September 2021 to March the next year, mostly on transmission lines (UCA News). Fisherman S.K. Cruz says fish, prawns and crabs moved away from shore because of turbine noise and vibration; he now travels about 15 nautical miles rather than 5 and his fuel costs have tripled. Hilda Anthony, 62, says her income from dried fish has ended (UCA News). The same report rejected the noise claim, saying no science shows airborne turbine noise affects fish. Rebecca Miranda of the Mannar Citizens Committee and residents told the Sunday Times of floods lasting four to five months over three years, submerged homes and farms, and lost crops and drumstick trees; they blame the project's raised road and line works for blocking outlets to the sea.
cases.outcome: The government paused the later wind project for a month in August 2025 to study local issues. Energy Minister Kumar Jayakody asked for a flood-risk report; the Ceylon Electricity Board reportedly promised drainage works, and Miranda says little has been done (Sunday Times).

cases.community: More than 10,000 people from 37 villages were moved between 2016 and 2020 into 11 new villages on high ground while low land was flooded. Residents told Radio Free Asia in 2021 they had houses but no farmland, apart from a few with land that did not flood; some forage in mountain forest and others slash and burn slopes to plant rice. One said there are no jobs and no income. Water runs short in the dry season, is untreated and must be boiled, and some must climb steep slopes to reach the river.
cases.outcome: A provincial official said authorities were looking for farmland, but finding 1,000 hectares near the dam is very difficult. A company employee said it was seeking land and other livelihoods such as raising chickens, ducks and pigs. The company replied on 26 February 2021 that resettlement finished by April 2018, that land distribution is complete with certificates issued to households moved to remote sites, and that compensation has been paid.

cases.point: Değirmenbaşı, İvrindi district (coordinates from Wikipedia). The complaint record does not name the mine; the village name matches İvrindi, site of one of the two Tümad mines. Approximate.

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
lenders.role: 40 million euro loan for Tümad's Lapseki (Çanakkale) and Ivrindi (Balıkesir) gold mines, project 49041, part of a US$200 million package with Akbank and Ziraat Bankası as parallel lenders.

cases.conditions: Bank loan to Tümad, a subsidiary of Nurol Holding, for mine development. The project planned vocational training and new jobs as alternative income.
cases.community: About 372 villagers from Değirmenbaşı told the bank's complaint office on 23 August 2020 that mining had taken over their grazing lands, so they could no longer live from livestock, and that the promised training and jobs did not materialise (EBRD IPAM).
cases.outcome: They asked only for problem-solving. The process ended on 7 September 2022 with no agreement (EBRD); Accountability Console records the complaint as withdrawn. No compliance review took place, so no office has ruled on the harm.

extend.note: Human Rights Watch Case Study B adds these accounts from opponents: THDC staff pressed some not to file with the Inspection Panel (complaint filed July 2012); about 35-50 people recognised as THDC staff and contractors confronted a community member during the Panel's 2013 visit, saying "We will kill you"; Durgapur protesters (25 February to 8 April 2015) say they were abused, threatened and photographed and their protest site destroyed; a widow says contractors destroyed her cattle shed and fruit trees in August 2014. THDC said there were no rights violations in the project area and that it would deal with incidents as necessary.

sources_add.title: At Your Own Risk: Reprisals against Critics of World Bank Group Projects

extend.note: Human Rights Watch adds reprisals: journalist Geoffrey Wokulira Ssebaggala was arrested around October 2009 for photographing police arresting residents, then received threatening calls from about January 2010; Uganda Land Alliance staff reported threats and surveillance; after Oxfam's September 2011 report officials sought a retraction, and in April 2012 the Ministry of Internal Affairs opened an investigation into the groups. The Alliance's Kampala office was burgled on 17 May 2014; the report says it is unclear whether this was tied to the eviction reporting.
